translations.text: After Saul died, David returned from defeating the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from Saul’s camp with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. When he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed before him.
David asked him, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “I escaped from the camp of Israel.”
David said to him, “What is the news? Tell me.” He said, “The people fled from the battle, and many of the people fell. Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead.”
David said to the young man, “Tell me how Saul and his son Jonathan died.”
The young man said to him, “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul leaning on his spear. The chariots and horsemen had caught up with him.”
He turned around, saw me, and called to me. I answered, ‘Here I am.’
He asked me, ‘Who are you?’ I told him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’
He said to me, ‘Stand over me and kill me, because convulsions have seized me, yet my life is still fully in me.’

“I stood over him and killed him, because I knew he would not survive after his fall. I took the crown that was on his head and the bracelet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.”
David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him.
They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the LORD’s people, and for the Israelites who had fallen by the sword.
David said to the young man who had brought him the news, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I am the son of an Amalekite who lives here as a foreigner.”
David said to him, “How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?”
David called one of the young men and said to him, “Come forward and strike him down.” He came forward, attacked him, and struck him, and he died.
David said to him, “Your blood is on your own head, because your own mouth testified against you when you said, ‘I killed the LORD’s anointed.’”
David sang this lament over Saul and his son Jonathan.
He ordered that the people of Judah be taught the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar:
O glory of Israel! The slain lie on your heights! How the mighty have fallen!
Do not tell it in Gath or announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised celebrate.
Mountains of Gilboa, may there be neither dew nor rain upon you, nor fields producing offerings! For there the shield of the mighty was broken, the shield of Saul, which was anointed with oil.
From the blood of the slain and the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s bow did not turn back, and Saul’s sword did not return empty.
Saul and Jonathan were loved and delightful in their lives, and in their death they were not separated. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who clothed you in scarlet over dyed garments and put gold ornaments on your clothing.
How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights!
I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan. You were very dear to me. Your love for me was more wonderful than the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!
Afterward David asked the LORD, “Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah?” The LORD said to him, “Go up.” David asked, “Where should I go?” He said, “To Hebron.”
David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
David and his men went up together, along with the members of his household, and they settled in Hebron.
The men of Judah came there to anoint David as king over the house of Judah. They told David, “The men of Jabesh-gilead buried Saul.”
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, “May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this kindness to your lord Saul by burying him.”
“Now may the LORD show you kindness and faithfulness. I too will show you kindness because you have done this.”
“Now let your hands be strong, and be courageous, for Saul your lord is dead, and the people of Judah have anointed me as king over them.”
Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him across to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, Geshur, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned for two years. But the house of Judah followed David.
The length of time that King David reigned in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s men went out and met the young men together at Gibeon. These young men sat on one side, and those young men on the other.
Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men get up and hold a contest before us.” Joab said, “Let them get up.”
They rose and crossed over in equal numbers: twelve from Benjamin belonging to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David’s men.
Each seized his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, and they fell together. They called that place in Gibeon the Field of Ambush.
The battle was very fierce that day, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by David’s servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was swift on his feet, like one of the gazelles in the wilderness.
Asahel pursued Abner, without turning aside to the right or to the left as he followed him.
Abner looked behind him and asked, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is.”
Abner said to him, “Turn aside to your right or your left, seize one of the young men, and take his weapons for yourself.” But Asahel would not turn aside from pursuing him.
Abner again told Asahel to turn aside from pursuing him. He said, “Stop pursuing me, or I will strike you and throw you to the ground. How could I then lift my face and look at your brother Joab?”

But he refused to turn aside, so Abner struck him in the chest with the butt of his spear, and it came out through his back. He fell there and died on the spot. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen stopped there.
Joab and Abishai set out and pursued Abner. The sun was setting when they reached the hill of Yamma, opposite Giah, on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites gathered behind Abner, formed a single company, and took their stand on top of a hill.

Abner called to Joab and said, “Will the sword keep killing forever? Don’t you know that the end will be bitter? How long will you wait before telling the men to turn back from pursuing their brothers?”
Joab said, “As the Lord lives, if you had not spoken, I would certainly have dismissed the men in the morning, each one from pursuing his brother.”
Joab sounded the trumpet, and all the men stopped. They no longer pursued Israel, and they did not fight any further.
Abner and his men traveled through the wilderness all that night. They crossed the Jordan, went toward Geshur, and came to Mahanaim.
Joab returned from pursuing Abner, and they gathered all the men. They counted twelve men of David’s forces who had been struck down, and Asahel was dead.
David’s men killed three hundred and sixty men from Benjamin and from Abner’s men.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Joab and his companions traveled all night, and dawn broke as they reached Hebron.
There was war between the house of Saul and the house of David. David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel.
His second was Caleb, by Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third was Absalom, the son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.
The fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith, and the fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital.
The sixth was Ithream, by Eglah, David’s wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was strengthening his position within the house of Saul.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Anah. Ish-bosheth said to Abner, “Why are you sleeping with my father’s concubine?”

Abner was very angry at Ish-bosheth’s words and said, “Am I a dog’s head belonging to Judah? Today I have shown kindness to the house of your father Saul, to his brothers, and to his friends. I have not handed you over to David, yet today you accuse me of wrongdoing over a woman!”
“May God do this to Abner, and more besides, if I do not do for David just as the Lord said to him:
to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and establish David’s throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
Ish-bosheth could not say another word in reply to Abner, because he was afraid of him.
Abner sent messengers to David, saying, “What is the land? Make your covenant with me, and my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you.”
David said, “Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing of you: you must not appear before me unless you bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, with you.”
David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul and said to him, “Give me my wife, whom I betrothed to myself for two hundred Philistine foreskins.”
Ish-bosheth sent for her and took her away from her husband, Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
Her husband went along, walking and weeping behind her as far as Bahurim. Abner said to him, “Go back,” and he went back.
Abner spoke to the elders of Israel and said to them, “For some time now you have wanted David to reign over you.
Now do so, because the Lord said concerning David, ‘Through my servant David I will save my people Israel from the power of the Philistines and from the power of all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke before the Benjaminites. Then Abner went to speak before David in Hebron about what pleased Israel and the whole house of Benjamin.
Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, and David prepared a great feast for Abner and the twenty men with him.

Abner said to David, “I will get up and go and gather all Israel to my lord the king. They will make a covenant with you, and you will rule over all that your heart desires.” David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
Just then David’s men and Joab returned from a raid, bringing a great deal of plunder with them. Abner was not with David at Hebron, because David had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
Joab and all the people with him arrived, and Joab was told, “Abner son of Ner came to King David, and he sent him away, and he went in peace.”
Joab came to King David and said to him, “What have you done? Abner came to you! Why did you send him away and let him leave you?
Don’t you know that Abner son of Ner came to deceive you, to learn your movements, and to find out everything you are doing?”
Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well of Sirah, but David did not know.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside inside the gate to speak with him privately. There he struck him in the abdomen, and he died, in revenge for the blood of Joab’s brother Asahel.
Afterward David heard about it and said, “I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the LORD of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May it rest on Joab’s head and on the head of his father’s entire household. May Joab’s household never lack someone with a discharge, someone with leprosy, someone who holds a spindle, someone who falls by the sword, or someone who lacks bread.”
Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in battle at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” King David and all the people walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king raised his voice and wept at Abner’s grave, and all the people wept.
The king mourned for Abner and said, “Did Abner die as Nabal died?”
“Your hands were not bound, and your feet did not enter chains. You fell as someone falls before wicked men.” And all the people wept over him again.
All the people urged David to eat bread while it was still daytime. But David swore, saying, “May God do this to me, and more besides, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets.”
All the people took notice and were pleased. Everything the king did was pleasing in the eyes of all the people.
That day all the people and all Israel knew that the killing of Abner son of Ner had not come from the king.
The king said, “Don’t you know that a great leader has fallen today in Israel?
“Today I am afraid, and I, the king, have seen that these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too harsh for me. May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil.”
When Ish-bosheth son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his hands grew weak, and all Israel was troubled.

Saul’s son had two men who were leaders of raiding bands. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, from the tribe of Benjamin, for Beeroth too was counted as belonging to Benjamin.
The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as resident foreigners to this day.

Jonathan son of Saul had a son whose feet were disabled. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, and as she hurried to escape, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, went to Ish-bosheth’s house in the heat of the day, while he was taking his midday sleep.
They came into the house and took some grains of wheat. Rechab and his brother Baanah struck him in the abdomen and escaped.
They entered the house while he was sleeping on his bed in his bedroom. They struck him and killed him, took his head, and traveled by the Arabah road all night.

They brought Ish-bosheth’s head to David at Hebron and said to King David, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy who sought your life. May the LORD grant our lord the king vengeance today on Saul and his descendants.”
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, saying, “As the LORD lives, who has rescued my life from every distress,
when someone informed me, saying, ‘Look, Saul is dead,’ and appeared to me as a bearer of good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag instead of giving him a reward for his news.
And now wicked men have killed a man in his own house on his bed! Now I will demand his blood from your hands and wipe you from the earth.”
David sent the young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung them on the hill in Hebron. They took Ish-bosheth’s head and buried it in Abner’s tomb in Hebron.
All the tribes of the house of Israel came to David at Hebron and said to him, “Look, we are your own flesh and bone.

Even in the past, when Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. The LORD said to you, ‘You will shepherd my people Israel, and you will be ruler over my people Israel.’”
All the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. They anointed David as king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned for forty years.
In Hebron he reigned over the house of Judah for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah for thirty-three years.

King David and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land. They said to David, “You will not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame.” They said, “David will not enter here.”
David captured the fortress of Zion, which is the City of David.

David said that day, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites and reaches the blind and the lame through the water channel—those whom David himself hates—[?].” That is why people say, “The blind and the lame must not enter the house.”
David lived in the fortress, which is Zion, and called it the City of David. David built around it on the inside.
David grew greater and greater, and the Lord, his God of hosts, was with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, along with cedar timber, carpenters, and stonemasons for building walls. They built a house for David.
David knew that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and that his kingdom had been exalted over his people Israel.
After coming from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to David.
These are the names of the sons born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, [?], Nathan, and Solomon.
And Ibhar [?], Elisha, Nepheg, and Japhia [?].
And Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
The Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, and all the Philistines went up to seek David. David heard about it and went down to the fortress.
The Philistines came and camped in the Valley of the Giants.
David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?” The LORD said to him, “Go up, because I will hand them over to you.”
David came to Baal-perazim and defeated them there. David said, “The LORD has broken through his enemies before me like water breaking through.” That is why he named that place Baal-perazim.
They abandoned their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.
The Philistines came up again and camped in the Valley of the Giants.
David inquired of the LORD, and the LORD said to him, “Do not go up. Instead, circle around behind them and come against them opposite Bachim.
When you hear the sound of marching on top of the mountain of Bachim, then act boldly, because the LORD will then go out before you to strike the Philistine army.”
David did just as the LORD had commanded him, and he defeated the Philistines from Geba as far as the entrance to Geder.
David again gathered all the troops of Israel, thirty thousand men.

David and all the people with him from among the men of Judah set out and went to Geba to bring up from there the ark of God, where the name of the LORD of hosts, who sits enthroned above the cherubim, was invoked.
They placed the ark of God on a new cart and took it from Abinadab’s house on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, Abinadab’s sons, were guiding the cart from behind.
They brought the ark of God from Abinadab’s house in Gibeah, and Ahio walked ahead of the ark.
David and the whole house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with cedar and cypress wood, with lyres, harps, [?], [?], and cymbals.
They came to the prepared threshing floors, and Uzzah reached out his hand toward the ark of the LORD and took hold of it because the oxen had stumbled.
The LORD’s anger burned against Uzzah, and the LORD struck him there because he had reached out his hand. He died there beside the ark of God.
David was distressed because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah, and he called that place “The Breach of Uzzah,” as it is called to this day.
David was afraid of the Lord that day and said, “How can I bring the ark of the Lord to me?”
David was unwilling to bring the ark of God to himself in the City of David. Instead, David diverted it to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom the Gittite and his entire household.

King David was told, “The LORD has blessed Obed-edom and everything he has because of the ark of the LORD.” So David went and joyfully brought the ark of the LORD up from Obed-edom’s house to the City of David.
When those carrying the ark of the Lord had walked six steps, David sacrificed fattened oxen.
David was praising the Lord with all his strength, and David was wearing a linen ephod.
David and all Israel were bringing up the ark of the Lord with shouts of joy and the sound of the trumpet.

The ark of the LORD was in David’s house. Michal, Saul’s daughter, looked out through the window and saw King David rejoicing and dancing before the ark of the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought the ark of the LORD and set it inside the tent David had pitched for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings to the Lord, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord Almighty.
He distributed to all the people, to the whole assembly of Israel, both men and women, one loaf of bread, one portion of meat, and one raisin cake each. Then all the people went home.

David turned to go home, and Michal, Saul’s daughter, came out to meet him. She said, “How dignified the king of Israel was today! He exposed himself today before the eyes of his servants’ slave women. You exposed yourself shamelessly, like one of the worthless fellows!”

David said to Michal, “It was before the LORD, who chose me over your father and his entire household and appointed me ruler over the LORD’s people, over Israel. It was for him that I made merry before the LORD.
I will become even less dignified than this and be lowly in my own eyes. But among the slave women you spoke of, I will be honored.”
Michal, Saul’s daughter, had no child until the day she died.
When the king was living in his house and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies,
The king said to Nathan the prophet, “Look, I live in a house of cedar, while the ark of God stays within curtains.”
Nathan said to the king, “Do everything you have in mind, for the Lord is with you.”
That very night the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, saying:
“Go and tell my servant David, ‘This is what the Lord says: You shall not build me a house to live in.
“For I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the Israelites up from the land of Egypt until today. Instead, I have traveled about in tents.

Wherever I traveled among all the Israelites, did I ever say a word to any of the tribes of Israel whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel? Did I ever say, ‘Why have you not built me a house of cedar?’
Now say this to my servant David: ‘This is what the LORD Almighty says: I took you from the sheepfold, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went, and I have destroyed all your enemies before you. I will make your name great, like the names of the great men of the earth.

I will provide a place for my people Israel, plant them there, and settle them peacefully in their own place. They will no longer be disturbed, and wicked people will no longer enslave them as they did before,
from the day I appointed you judge over my people Israel. I have given you rest from all your enemies. The LORD has made known to you that the LORD will establish a house for you.
When your days are complete and you lie down with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, one who comes from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom.
He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be his father, and he will be my son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with a human rod and with blows such as people give.
But I will not take my faithful love away from him as I took it away from Saul, who was before you and whom I removed from my presence.
Your house and your kingdom will be secure before me forever, and your throne will be established before me forever.
Nathan the prophet told David all these words and this entire vision.
King David came and sat before the LORD and said, “Who am I, LORD God, and what is my household, that you have brought me this far?
Yet this was a small thing in your eyes, LORD God, for you have spoken about your servant’s household far into the future. This is instruction for humanity, LORD God.
What more can your servant David say to you? You yourself know your servant, Lord God.
For the sake of your words and according to your own heart, you have done all this great work to make it known to your servant.
Therefore you are great, LORD God, because there is no one like you, and there is no God besides you, according to everything we have heard with our own ears.

Who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem as a people for himself, to make a name for himself, and to perform great things and wonders for them on the earth, as in former times for your people whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt—a people whose God you are?
You established your people Israel for yourself to be your people forever, and you, Lord, became their God.
Now, LORD God, confirm forever the word you have spoken about your servant and his household, and do as you have said.
May your name be great forever, as you have said, LORD Almighty, God of Israel. May the household of your servant David be established before you forever.
For you, LORD Almighty, God of Israel, have revealed this to your servant, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found it in his heart to pray this prayer before you.
Now, LORD God, you are God. May your words prove true, for you have promised this good thing to your servant.
Now begin to bless your servant’s household, so that it may remain before you forever. For you, LORD God, have spoken, and through your blessing may your servant’s household be blessed forever.”
After this, David struck the Philistines and defeated them, and David took Ramath-gamma from the Philistines.

He defeated the Moabites and measured them with ropes, making them lie down on the ground. He measured two rope lengths to be put to death and one full rope length to be kept alive. The Moabites became David’s servants and brought tribute.
David struck Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when he went to restore his control at the Euphrates River.
David struck down seventeen hundred of his charioteers and twenty thousand foot soldiers. David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but kept enough for a hundred chariots.
Edom and Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, and David struck down twenty-two thousand men of Edom.
David appointed officials in Edom and Damascus. The Edomites became David’s servants and paid tribute. The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.
David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer’s servants. King David also took a very large quantity of bronze and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Tebah and Berothai, the towns of Hadadezer.
Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated Hadadezer’s entire army.

Toi sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and congratulate him because he had fought Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer was a warlike man. Joram son of Toi took silver vessels, gold vessels, and bronze vessels with him and brought them to David.
King David also dedicated these to the Lord, together with the silver and gold that he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued:
from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, the Amalekites, and the dominion of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David fought a battle there when he returned after defeating Edom in the Valley of Salt. He struck down eighteen thousand there.
David appointed officials throughout Edom, and all the Edomites became David’s servants. The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.
David reigned over all Israel, administering justice and righteousness for all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded the army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Zadok son of Ahitub the Gilonite and Abiathar son of Ahimelech were priests, and Seraiah was the scribe.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the nobles and the soldiers, and David’s sons were high officials.
David said, “Is there still anyone left from the house of Saul, so that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
Saul’s household had a servant named Ziba. They summoned him to David, and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He answered, “I am your servant.”
The king said to him, “Is there anyone still left from Saul’s household to whom I can show mercy for God’s sake?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan has a son still living, whose feet are disabled.”
The king asked him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “He is at the house of Machir son of Gamal, in Lo-debar.”
The king sent for him and brought him from the house of Machir son of Gamal in Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David, fell facedown, and bowed before him. David said to him, “Mephibosheth!” He answered, “Your servant has come.”

David said to him, “Do not be afraid, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the fields of your forefather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.”
He bowed and said, “What is your servant worth, that you have taken notice of me, a dead dog?”
The king summoned Ziba and said to him, “Everything that belonged to Saul and his entire household I have given to your master’s son.

“You, your sons, and your servants are to cultivate the land for him and bring in food for your master’s son to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master’s son, will always eat at my table.” Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, “Your servant will do everything that my lord the king has commanded his servant.” Mephibosheth ate at the king’s table like one of the king’s sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Micah. Everyone living in Ziba’s household became Mephibosheth’s servants.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table. Both his feet were disabled.
Afterward, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place.

David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” David sent his servants to comfort him over his father’s death. David’s servants came to the land of the Ammonites.

The Ammonite leaders said to their lord Hanun, “Do you think David is honoring your father by sending you men to comfort you? Hasn’t David sent his servants to you to spy on the city, investigate it, and overthrow it?”
Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved off half their beards, cut their tunics with arrows as far as their buttocks, and sent them away.
David was told, and he sent men to meet them, because the men were deeply ashamed. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”

The Ammonites saw that they had offended David. They sent and hired Edom son of Rehob and Edom son of Zobah, twenty thousand foot soldiers, along with a thousand men from the king of Maacah and twelve thousand foot soldiers from Tob.
When David heard this, he sent Joab and the entire army of warriors.
The Ammonites came out and drew up for battle at the entrance to the gate. [?] Edom son of Rehob, Edom son of Zobah, Tob, and Maacah were by themselves in the open country.
Joab saw that battle was arrayed against him both in front and behind. He selected men from all the chosen men of Israel and drew them up against Edom.
He entrusted the rest of the troops to his brother Abishai, who drew them up against the Ammonites.
He said to his brother Abishai, “If Edom is too strong for me, come to my aid. If the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come and help you.”
“Let us be strong and take our battle positions for our people and for the towns of our God. May the Lord do what is good in his eyes.”
Joab and the troops with him advanced to fight Edom, and they fled before him.
When the Ammonites saw that Edom had fled, they too fled before Abishai and entered the town. Joab turned back from the Ammonites and went to Jerusalem.
When Edom saw that they had been defeated before Israel, they gathered together.
Hadadezer sent and brought out the Edomites who were beyond the river. They came to Helam, with Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, leading them.

David was informed, and he gathered all Israel. They crossed the Jordan and came to Helam, with Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, leading them. Edom drew up in battle formation against Israel, and David fought against Edom.

Edom fled before Israel, and David killed seventeen hundred charioteers, four thousand horsemen, and many other men of Edom. He also struck down Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, and he died there.
All Hadadezer’s servants saw that they had been defeated before the Israelites. They made peace with Israel and served them, and the Edomites were afraid to help the Ammonites again.
At the turn of the year, at the time when the king went out on campaign, David sent Joab, his servants with him, and all Israel. They laid siege to Rabbah, while David remained in Jerusalem.
Toward evening, David rose from his bed and walked about on the roof of his royal palace. He saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful.
David sent to inquire about the woman. They said, “This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Ahinoam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite.”
David sent a messenger and brought her. She came to him, and he slept with her after she had bathed to cleanse herself from her menstrual impurity. Then she returned and went to her house.
The woman became pregnant. She sent word to David and told him, “I am pregnant.”
David sent word to Joab, saying, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” Joab sent Uriah the Hittite to David.
Uriah came to David, and David asked Uriah about Joab, the people, and the war.
David said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah left the king’s palace, and a gift from the king followed him.
Uriah slept at the king’s gate beside all his master’s servants and did not go down to his house.
They told David that Uriah had not gone down to his house. David said to Uriah, “You have just come from a journey. Why did you not go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David, “The ark of the Lord’s covenant, Israel, and Judah are staying in shelters, and my lord Joab and my lord’s servants are camping in the open fields. Should I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? No! By your life and by your very soul, I will not do such a thing.”
David said to Uriah, “Stay here today, and tomorrow I will send you away.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him, and he ate and drank in his presence and became drunk. In the evening he went out and slept beside his lord’s servants, but he did not go down to his house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by Uriah’s hand.
He wrote to him, “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest fighting, and withdraw from behind him so that he will be struck down and die.”
While Joab was besieging the city, he stationed Uriah in a place where he knew there were strong warriors.
The men of the town came out and fought against Joab. Some of the troops, David’s servants, fell there, and Uriah the Hittite also died.
Joab sent word to David and reported everything that had happened in the battle.
Joab instructed the messenger, saying to him, “When you have finished telling the king everything that happened in the battle,
“If the king’s anger rises and he says to you, ‘Why did you approach the town to fight against it? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall?’”

“‘Who killed Abimelech son of Nedubbaal? Was it not a woman who threw a piece of an upper millstone down on him from the wall, so that he died? Why did you approach the wall?’ If he says these things to you, tell him, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.’”
The messenger went and told David everything Joab had instructed him to say.
The messenger said to David, “The men were too strong for us and came out against us into the open field, but we pressed them back as far as the town gate.”
Those stationed on the wall shot at us, and some of your servants died, O king. Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.”
David said to the messenger, “Tell Joab, ‘Do not be distressed about this, for such things happen in war, one way or another. Press the attack against the town, capture it, and destroy it.’”
The wife of Uriah the Hittite heard that her husband had died, and she mourned for her husband.
When her days of mourning were over, David sent and brought her into his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done was evil in the Lord’s sight.
The Lord sent Nathan the prophet to David. He came to him and said, “There were two men in one town, one rich and the other poor.”
The rich man had very many sheep and cattle.

“The poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb that he had acquired. It lived with him and his children together. It ate from his bread, drank from his cup, and slept in his lap. It was like a daughter to him.”

A traveler came to a rich man, but he was unwilling to take any of his own cattle or sheep to prepare a meal for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man's ewe lamb and prepared it for the traveler who had come to him.
Then David became angry with the man and said, "As the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die!"
He must repay four lambs for the one, because he did this and showed no pity.”
Nathan said to David, "You are the man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I anointed you to reign over my people Israel, and I rescued you from Saul's hands.

I gave you your master's daughters, and I laid your master's wives in your arms. I gave you the daughters of Israel and Judah. If these were too few, you could have spoken, and I would have added as many again, and as many again.

Why have you despised the LORD's command and done what is evil before the LORD? You killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
From now on, the sword will never leave your household, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.

This is what the LORD says: Look, I am raising up trouble against you from within your own household. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your companion, and he will sleep with them in the sight of this sun."
You acted secretly, but I will do this in the sight of all Israel and in broad daylight.’”
David said to Nathan, "I have sinned before the LORD." Nathan said to David, "The LORD has also taken away your sin. You will not die.
Nevertheless, because you have emboldened the LORD's enemies by this deed, the son born to you by her will certainly die."
Nathan went home, and the LORD struck the child whom Uriah the Hittite’s wife had borne to David, and he became seriously ill.
David pleaded with God for the child. David fasted, spent the night fasting, and lay on the ground.
The elders of his household stood beside him to raise him from the ground, but he refused and would not eat with them.

On the seventh day, the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him that the child had died, for they said, "While the child was alive, we spoke to him, but he would not listen to us. How can we now tell him that the child has died? He may do something harmful."
When David saw his servants whispering, he realized that the child had died. David said to his servants, "Has the child died?" They told him, "He has died."

David got up from the ground, washed, anointed himself with oil, and changed his clothes. He entered the house of the LORD and worshiped. Then he came to his own house and asked for food. They set it before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, "What is this you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted and pleaded, but when he died, you got up and ate food."
David said to them, "While the child was alive, I fasted and pleaded because I said, 'Who knows whether God will have mercy on him and the child will live?'
But now that he has died, why should I fast? Can he return again? I am going to him, but he cannot come to me."
David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He went in to her and slept with her, and she gave birth to a son and named him Solomon. The LORD loved the child.
He sent for Nathan the prophet, who named him Jedidiah, because the LORD loved him.
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David and said, “I have fought against Rabbah and have also captured the royal city.
Now gather the rest of the people, come and camp against the city, and capture it. Otherwise, I may capture the city myself, and it will be called by my name.
David gathered all the people, went against Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.
He took their king's crown from his head. It weighed a talent of gold and contained precious stones. It was placed on David's head, and he brought a very great amount of plunder out of the city.

He brought out the people who were in it, put them in iron collars and chains, and made them pass under the measuring line. He did the same to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After this, Absalom son of David had a sister named Tamar, and Amnon son of David fell in love with her.
Amnon became distressed over his sister Tamar because she was a virgin, and Amnon could not say anything to her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
He said to Amnon, "Son of the king, why do you go on like this morning after morning? Won't you tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I am in love with Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom."

Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, tell him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and feed me. Let her make cakes for me where I can see, and let me eat from her hands.'"
Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick, and the king came to see him. Amnon said to the king, "Let my sister Tamar come to me and make two cakes before my eyes, so that I may eat from her hands."
David sent word to Tamar, saying, “Go to your brother Amnon and prepare food for him.”
Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, and made cakes.
She took the cakes and set them before him, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, "Have everyone leave me." So everyone left him.
Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom for me, so that I may eat from your hands.” Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the bedroom to her brother Amnon.
She brought them to him to eat, but he seized her and said to her, “Come, sleep with me, my sister.”
She said to him, “No, my brother! Do not dishonor me. Such a thing must not be done in Israel.
“Where could I take my disgrace? And you would be regarded as one of the fools in Israel. Now speak to the king; he will not withhold me from you.”
But he would not listen to her. He seized her, overpowered her, slept with her, and dishonored her.
Then Amnon hated her intensely. The hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. Amnon said to her, “Get up and go!”
She said to him, “Now that you have done this great evil to me, are you sending me away?” But he would not listen to her.
He called the young man who served him and said to him, “Put this woman outside, away from me, and shut the door in her face.”
Tamar took ashes and put them on her head. She tore the embroidered tunic she was wearing, put her hands on her head, and went away wailing.

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon slept with you? Now, my sister, keep quiet; he is your brother. Do not take this matter to heart.” So Tamar stayed in her brother Absalom’s house, desolate.
King David heard about all these things and was deeply distressed.
Absalom said nothing to Amnon, either good or bad, because Absalom hated Amnon for dishonoring his sister Tamar.
When the season came, Absalom had sheep shearers at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king’s sons.
Absalom came to the king and said to him, “Your servant has sheep shearers at work. Let the king and his servants come with your servant.”
He said to him, “No, my son. We should not all go, or we will be a burden to you.” Absalom urged him, but he would not go with him. He did, however, give him his blessing.
Absalom said to him, “Then why should my brother Amnon not go with me?” The king said to him, “Why should he go with you?”
But Absalom urged him, and he sent Amnon and all the king’s sons with him.

Absalom commanded his servants, saying to them, “When Amnon is cheerful from the wine and I tell you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ kill him. Do not be afraid. I myself have commanded you. Be strong and act like men.”
Absalom’s servants did as Absalom had commanded them. Then all the king’s sons got up, each mounted his mule, and they fled.
While they were still on the road, news reached David that Absalom had killed all the king’s sons and had not left a single one of them.
The king got up, tore his clothes, and lay on the ground. All his servants stood there with their clothes torn.

Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah, spoke up and said to him, “Let my lord the king not suppose that all the king’s sons have died. Only Amnon is dead. Absalom had resolved on this from the day Amnon dishonored his sister Tamar.”
“So now, let my lord the king not suppose that all the king’s sons have died. Only Amnon is dead.”
Absalom fled. The lookout raised his eyes and saw many people coming along the road from the side of the mountain.
Jonadab said to the king, “Look, the king’s sons have arrived! It has happened just as your servant said.”
As he finished speaking, the king’s sons arrived. They raised their voices and wept, and the king and all his servants also wept bitterly.
Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. David mourned for his son for many days.
Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and he stayed there for three years.
King David stopped pursuing Absalom, because he had been comforted over Amnon's death.
Joab son of Zeruiah knew that King David's heart had turned toward Absalom.

Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there. He said to her, “Act as a mourner. Put on mourning clothes and do not anoint yourself with oil. Be like a woman who has been mourning for the dead for many days.”
Go in to the king and say this to him." Joab prepared the words and put them in her mouth.
The woman from Tekoa came to the king, fell facedown on the ground, bowed before him, and said, “Save me, my lord the king!”
The king said to her, "What is wrong?" She said to him, "I am indeed a widow; my husband is dead.
“Your servant had two sons. The two of them fought in the field, and there was no one to separate them. One overpowered the other and killed him.”

“Now the whole clan has risen against your servant. They say, ‘Hand over the one who killed his brother, so that we may kill him for the brother he murdered.’ They want to destroy the heir. They want to extinguish the ember that is left to me, leaving his father neither a name nor descendants on the face of the earth.”
The king said to her, "Go home. I will give orders concerning you."
The woman from Tekoa said to the king, “My lord the king, let this guilt rest on me and on my father’s household. Let the king and his throne be free of blame.”
The king said to her, "Bring me anyone who says anything to you, and he will not approach you again."

She said, “Let my lord the king remember that the LORD your God does not destroy through repeated blood vengeance [?]. Do not let them destroy my son.” The king said to her, “As the LORD God lives, not a hair from your son’s head will fall to the ground.”
The woman said, "May your servant say something to the king?" The king said to her, "Speak."
The woman said to him, “Why have you planned such a thing against God’s people? And why have you spoken, O king, like a guilty man, when you, O king, do not bring back your banished one?”
“We must surely die. We are like water poured out on the ground that cannot be gathered up again. Yet God does not take away life, but devises a plan so that no one will be banished from him.”
Now I have spoken this matter to my lord the king because the people frightened me. Your servant said, ‘I will speak to the king.’
Perhaps he will rescue his servant from the hands of those who would destroy both me and my son from God's inheritance.'

Your servant said, ‘May the word of my lord the king be confirmed, and may it be an offering, for my lord the king is like an angel of God in hearing good and evil. May the Lord your God be with you.’
The king answered the woman, ‘Do not hide anything from me that I ask you.’ The woman said to him, ‘Let my lord the king speak.’

The king said to her, ‘Is Joab’s hand with you in all this?’ The woman answered him, ‘As you live, my lord the king, you have not turned either right or left from anything my lord the king has said. Your servant Joab instructed me, and he put all these words into the mouth of your servant.’
‘Your servant Joab did this so that you would act on my behalf. My lord is wise, with the wisdom of the angels of God, knowing everything that is in the land.’
The king said to Joab, "Look, I have done as you said. Go and bring the young man Absalom to me."

Joab fell facedown on the ground, bowed, and blessed the king. Joab said, ‘Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because the king has done what his servant asked.’
Joab set out and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, ‘Let him go to his house, but he must not appear before me.’ So Absalom went to his house and did not see the king’s face.
There was no man in Israel as highly praised as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, there was no blemish in him.
Whenever he cut the hair of his head—he would cut it from time to time because it became heavy on him—he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels by the king’s weight.
Three sons and one daughter were born to Absalom. Her name was Tamar, and she too was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two years without seeing the king.
Absalom sent for Joab to send him to the king, but Joab was unwilling to come. He sent again a second time, but Joab was unwilling to come.
Absalom said to his servants, ‘Look at Joab’s field beside mine, with wheat or barley in it. Go and set it on fire.’ So Absalom’s servants burned Joab’s field.
Joab got up and went to Absalom’s house. Joab said to Absalom, ‘Why have your servants set my field on fire?’

Absalom said to Joab, ‘Look, I sent for you and said, “Come, so that I can send you to the king to ask, ‘Why did I come from Geshur? I would have been better off staying there.’” Now I want to appear before the king. If I am guilty, let him kill me.’
Joab came before the king and told him what Absalom had said. The king summoned Absalom, and Absalom came before the king and bowed facedown on the ground before him. Then the king kissed Absalom.
Afterward, Absalom acquired chariots and horsemen for himself, and fifty couriers who ran before him.

Absalom would rise early and stand beside the king’s gate. Whenever anyone had a case to be judged before the king, Absalom would call him over and ask him, ‘What town are you from?’ He would answer, ‘Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel.’
Absalom would say to him, ‘Look, I see that your arguments are good and right, but there is no one appointed by the king to hear you.’
Absalom would say, ‘If only someone would make me a judge in the land! Then everyone who had a case or a claim would come to me, and I would rule in his favor.’
Whenever a man stood before him to bow down to him, he would take him by the hand and kiss him.
Absalom did this to all the Israelites who came for judgment before the king, and Absalom turned away the hearts of all the people of Israel.
After four years, Absalom said to the king, “Let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow I made to the Lord.
‘For your servant made a vow while I was living in Geshur and in Edom: “If the Lord will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the Lord.”’
The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he set out and went to Hebron.
Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel and instructed them, ‘When you hear the sound of the trumpet, say, “Absalom has become king in Hebron!”’
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They went innocently, knowing nothing about it.

Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, and brought him from his town, Giloh, while he was offering sacrifices. The rebellion kept growing stronger, and the people on Absalom’s side became very numerous.
A messenger came to David and told him, “The hearts of the Israelites are united behind Absalom.”

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, ‘Get up! Let us flee, or we may not be able to escape from Absalom. Let us leave quickly, or he may hurry and overtake us, bring disaster upon us, and put the city to the sword.’
The king’s servants said to the king, “Whatever you wish, our lord the king, your servants will do.”
The king went out, with all his household following him. The king left ten women, his concubines, to look after his house.
The king went out, with all the people following him, and they stopped some distance away.
All his servants passed by him, along with all his free men and all his workers. All the Gittites who had followed him from Gath passed before the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why are you also going with us? Stay behind, apart from the king, for you are a foreigner and have been exiled from your own country.”
“You arrived yesterday, and today should we make you wander about with us? I am going wherever I can go. Stay behind and settle your brothers comfortably.”
Ittai answered the king, “As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, O king, wherever my lord the king may be, whether in death or in life, your servant will be there.”
David said to Ittai, “Go on across.” So Ittai the Gittite crossed over, together with all his men and all the households with him.
The whole land wept bitterly as all the people crossed over. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people crossed over toward the road to the wilderness.
Zadok the priest was also there, with all the Levites who were with him, carrying the ark of God. Abiathar went up until all the people had finished crossing out of the city.
The king said to Zadok, “Take the ark of God back to the city. Perhaps I will find favor in the Lord’s eyes, and he will bring me back and let me see it and its dwelling place.”
But if he says, ‘I take no pleasure in you,’ here I stand. Let him do to me whatever seems good to him.”
The king said to Zadok the priest, “Go back to the city in peace, you and Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar—both your sons with you.”
Look, I will wait in the plain of the wilderness until someone comes from you and brings me word.”
So Zadok and Abiathar the priests took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up and walked along with his head covered. All the people with him covered their heads and went up weeping.
They informed David, saying, “Ahithophel has joined Absalom’s rebellion.” David said, “May the Lord frustrate Ahithophel’s counsel.”
David reached a certain place where he used to worship God. Hushai the Archite came to him with his tunic torn and dust on his head.
David said to him, “If you cross over with me, you will be a burden to me.
“But return to the city and say to Absalom, ‘I am your servant, O king, and formerly I was your father’s servant.’ And now I, the king, ask you: go and frustrate Ahithophel’s counsel.”
“Zadok and Abiathar the priests are there with you. Tell Zadok and Abiathar the priests everything you hear from the king’s household.”
“Their two sons are there, Ahimaaz the son of Zadok and Jonathan the son of Abiathar. Send me through them everything you hear.”
So Hushai, David’s friend, went to the city, and Absalom entered Jerusalem.

David had gone a little beyond the place where he used to worship when Ziba, Mephibosheth’s servant, came to meet him. He brought with him two loaded donkeys carrying two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred cakes of figs, a hundred cheeses, and a skin of wine.

The king said to Ziba, “Where did you get these?” Ziba answered him, “The donkeys are to carry the baggage of the king’s household, the bread and cheeses are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who become exhausted in the wilderness to drink.”
The king said to him, “Where is your master’s son?” Ziba answered him, “He is staying in Jerusalem, saying, ‘The Israelites will restore to me the kingdom of my father Saul.’”
David said to Ziba, “Everything belonging to Mephibosheth is given to you.” Ziba said, “I have much, and I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king.”
King David came as far as Bahurim. A man from the clan of Saul’s household came out from there. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and he came out cursing David.
He threw stones at him and at all his servants, at all the people, and at all his servants on his right and on his left.
As Shimei cursed David, he said to him, “Get out! Get out, you bloodshedder, you wicked man!”

“May the Lord repay you for all the blood of Saul’s household, whose place you took as king. May the Lord hand your kingdom over to your son Absalom. Now you have been repaid for your wickedness, because you are a bloodshedder.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah said to David, “Why is this dead dog cursing my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head.”
King David said to him, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse. The Lord himself told him to curse David. Who, then, can say to me, ‘Why has he treated me this way?’”

David said to Abishai and all his servants, “Look, my son, who came from my own body, is seeking to take my life. And now the Benjaminites too! Leave him alone and let him curse; God himself has told him to.”
“Perhaps the Lord will look upon my oppression and repay me with good in place of the curses directed at me today.”
David and his servants continued along the road, while Shimei went along the hillside opposite him, cursing him, throwing stones at him, and flinging dust at him.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted, and they rested there.
Absalom, all the people with him, and all Israel came to Jerusalem, with Ahithophel accompanying him.
When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?”
Hushai said to Absalom, “No! I belong to the one whom the LORD, this people, and all Israel have chosen, and I will stay with him.
And I will belong to him. And secondly, whose servant am I? Was it not in my hands [?]? Just as I served your father, so I will serve you.”
Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Advise me. What should I do?”

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Go and sleep with your father’s concubines, whom he left to look after his house. When all Israel hears that you have been with your father’s concubines, everyone who is with you will be strengthened.”
They pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days, the advice Ahithophel gave was regarded as though someone had consulted the word of God. That was how all Ahithophel’s advice was regarded by both David and Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, “I will choose twelve thousand men and set out to pursue David by night.
I will catch up with him while he is exhausted and his hands are weak, and I will throw him into panic. All the people with him will flee, and I will kill the king alone.”
I will bring all the people back to you, as everyone you wanted returns, and all the people will be at peace.
The proposal pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite, and let us hear what he has to say as well.”
Hushai came to Absalom, and Absalom said to him, “This is what Ahithophel has said. Should we do what he says? If not, you tell us.”
Hushai said to Absalom, “The advice Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai said to him, “You know your father and his servants: they are mighty warriors, and they are bitter in spirit, like a bear bereaved of her cubs in the wilderness. Your father is a man of war and will not spend the night beside the people.
He is now hiding in one of the places or in one of the locations. When some of them fall at the outset and the news is heard that there has been a slaughter among Absalom’s followers,
even a mighty warrior whose heart is like a lion’s heart will completely lose courage, because all Israel knows that your father is a mighty warrior and that those with him are brave fighting men.
I advise that, when all Israel has gathered to you from Dan as far as Beersheba, you go in their midst.
We will come upon him in whatever place he is found, and we will descend upon him as dew falls on the ground. We will not leave even one of all the men with him alive.
If he enters a town, all Israel will throw ropes around it and drag it down to the valley, leaving not even a pebble there.”

Absalom and all Israel said, “Hushai the Archite’s advice is better than Ahithophel’s advice.” The LORD had decreed that Ahithophel’s good advice should be frustrated, so that the LORD might bring disaster upon Absalom.
Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, “This is what Ahithophel advised Absalom and all Israel, and this is what I advised.
Now send word quickly to David and tell him, ‘Do not spend the night in the plain of the wilderness. Cross over, so that you and all the people with you will not perish.’”
Nathan and Ahimaaz were staying beside the Fuller’s Spring. A servant girl went and informed them, and they went and informed King David, because they could not risk being seen entering the city.
A young man saw them and told Absalom. The two of them went and entered the house of a man from Bahurim. He had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.
The woman took a covering and spread it over the well, and spread crushed grain on it. No one knew about it.

Absalom’s servants came to the woman’s house and asked, “Where are Ahimaaz and Nathan?” The woman told them, “They have gone on from here because they were looking for water.” They did not find them and returned to Jerusalem.

After they had gone, the two men climbed out of the well and went to inform King David. They said to him, “Get up quickly and cross the water, because this is what Ahithophel has advised against you.”
David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By dawn, not a single person remained who had not crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been accepted, he saddled his donkey and set out for his home in his own town. He put his household affairs in order, hanged himself, and died. He was buried in his father’s tomb.
David crossed over to Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan with all Israel.
Absalom appointed Amasa over the army in Joab’s place. Amasa was the son of an Israelite named Ithra, who had slept with Abigail daughter of Nahash, the sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
Israel and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Abishai son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Gamiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Doblin
brought beds, bedding, pottery, wheat, barley, roasted grain, flour, beans, and lentils.
They also brought honey, butter, sheep, and cheese made from cows’ milk for David and the people with him to eat, because they said, “The people are hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.”
David counted the people with him and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds over them.
A third with Joab, a third with Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third with Ittai the Gittite. The king said to the people,

“If we flee, they will pay no attention to us. For now, ten thousand are enough for us. It is better for us to have reinforcements from the towns.” David’s servants said to him, “We will go out and hurry to fight them.”
The king said to them, “Do whatever seems good to you.” The king stood beside the gate, and all the people went out in units of hundreds and thousands.
The king commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, “Capture the young man Absalom alive for me.” All the people heard the king give all the commanders these orders concerning Absalom.
The people went out into the open country to meet Israel, and the battle began.
The people of Israel were defeated there by David’s servants, and there was a great slaughter there: twenty thousand.
The battle spread very widely across the land, and the wild animals of the forest devoured more of the people that day than the sword killed.

Absalom encountered David’s servants. Absalom was riding a mule, and the mule went under the branches of a large terebinth. Absalom’s head became caught in the large terebinth, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule beneath him went on.
A man saw him and told Joab, saying, “I saw Absalom hanging in an oak.”
Joab said to the man who had told him, “When you saw him, why did you not strike him down to the ground? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a garment.”

The man said to Joab, “Even if you had counted out and given me a thousand pieces of silver, I would not have raised my hand against the king’s son. For in my presence the king commanded you, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, ‘Take care of the young man Absalom for me.’
If I had done it, I would have been guilty at the cost of my own life. Nothing would have been hidden from the king, and you would have stood against me.”
Joab said to him, “I will not linger here with you like this.” Joab took three rods in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart while he was still alive and hanging in the terebinth.
Then ten young men who carried Joab’s weapons turned on Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Joab sounded the trumpet, and the troops who had been pursuing Israel turned back, because Joab restrained the troops.
They took Absalom and threw him into a pit, into a large hollow, and raised a great heap of large stones over him. All Israel fled, each to his own tent.

While Absalom was still alive, he had set up a statue for himself in the Valley of the Kings, because he said, “I have no one to keep my name alive.” He named the statue after himself, and it is called Absalom’s Monument to this day.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, “Let me run and bring the king the good news that the Lord has vindicated him against his enemies.”
Joab said to him, “You should not carry the news today. Carry news another day, but do not carry it today, because the news you would be bringing is that the king’s son is dead.”
Joab said to the Cushite, “Go, tell the king what you have seen.”

Ahimaaz son of Zadok ran again and said to Joab, “Whatever happens, let me also run and follow the Cushite.” Joab said to him, “Why should you run, my son, when no one will give you anything for the news?”
He said to him, “Whatever happens, let me run.” He said to him, “Run.” So Ahimaaz ran by the road through the plain and overtook the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates. The lookout went onto the roof of the gate in the wall, looked up, and saw a man running alone.
The lookout called out and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, he has news to tell.” The man kept coming and drew near.
The watchman called toward the gate and said, “Look, another man is running alone!”
The lookout said, “I see that the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” The king said, “He is a good man, and he is coming with good news.”

The king called to Ahimaaz and said to him, “You have arrived safely.” He bowed before the king with his face to the ground and said, “Blessed is the LORD your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hands against my lord the king.”

The king said to him, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” Ahimaaz said to him, “I saw a large army drawn up against Joab, the servant of my lord the king, and against your servant. I did not know what it was.”
The king said to him, “Stand here.” So he turned aside and stood there.
Then the Cushite arrived and said, “Let my lord the king receive the good news: today the LORD has vindicated him against everyone who has risen against him.”
The king said to the Cushite, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” The Cushite said, “May your enemies, my lord the king, and everyone who has risen against you to harm you, be like that young man.”
The king was deeply distressed and went up to the chamber and wept. As he wept, he kept saying, “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died in your place, Absalom, my son!”
Joab was told, “The king is weeping and mourning for Absalom.”
That day became a day of mourning for all the people, because the people heard that day that the king was grieving over his son.
The people slipped into the city that day as people slip away in shame when they flee from battle.
The king covered his face and cried out loudly, saying, “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom!”
Joab came to the king and said to him, “Today you have shamed all your servants, who today saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, your wives, and your concubines.

You have loved those who hate you and hated those who love you. Today you have shown that neither nobles nor servants mean anything to you. I know today that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, you would be pleased.

Now get up, go out, and speak to your servants. For I swear by the Lord that if you do not go out, not one man will stay with you tonight. This will be worse for you than all the troubles that have come upon you from your youth until now.”

The king got up and sat at the gate. They informed all the people, saying, “Look, the king is sitting at the gate.” All the people came before the king. Meanwhile, the Israelites had fled, each to his own tent.

All the people throughout all the tribes of Israel were discussing this and saying, “The king rescued us from the power of all our enemies, and he saved us from the power of the Philistines. Now come, let us flee the land after Absalom.
For Absalom, whom we anointed and appointed over us, has died in battle.” They said to one another, “Why, then, are you keeping silent about returning with the king?”
Come, let us bring him back to his home.” The words of all the Israelites reached the king.
He said to them, “You are my brothers, my own flesh and bone. Why have you been the last to return with the king?”
He said to Amasa, “Look, you are my own flesh and bone. May God do this to me, and more besides, if you do not become commander of the army in my service for all time in place of Joab.”
He won over the hearts of everyone in the house of Judah as though they were one man. They sent word to the king, saying, “Return, you and all your servants.”
The king returned and came as far as the Jordan. The people of Judah came to Gilgal to go and meet the king and bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, a Benjaminite, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
Ziba, Saul’s servant, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, crossed over and made a bridge across the Jordan before the king.
They made crossings to bring the king’s household across and to do whatever pleased him. Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king as he crossed the Jordan.
He said to the king, “My lord, do not hold me guilty, and do not remember the wrong your servant did on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. May my lord the king not take it to heart.
I, your servant, know that I have sinned. Look, today I have come first of all the house of Joseph and have come down to meet my lord the king.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, “Should Shimei not be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?”
David said, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should become my adversaries today? No one in Israel shall die today. Do I not know today that I am king over Israel?”
The king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” And the king swore an oath to him.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came down to meet the king. He had not trimmed his beard or changed his clothes from the day the king left until the day the king returned safely.
When he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?”
Mephibosheth said to him, “My lord the king, my servant deceived me. For I told him, ‘Put me on the donkey so that I can ride it and go with my lord the king,’ because your servant is lame.
My servant spoke falsely about me, my lord the king. But you, my lord the king, are like an angel of God. Do whatever seems right to you.

For my father’s entire household deserved death at your hands, my lord the king, yet you counted your servant among those who eat at your table. So now I cannot plead my case or even speak before my lord the king.”
The king said to him, “You have said enough. I have decided that you and Ziba are to divide the fields.”
Mephibosheth said to the king, “Let the servant take it all, now that my lord the king has come home safely.”
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Doblin and crossed the Jordan with the king to see him off from there.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years old. He had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim, because he was a wealthy man.
The king said to Barzillai, “You too, cross over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem.”
Barzillai said to the king, “How many years of life do I have left, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

“I am now eighty years old, and I cannot distinguish between good and bad. Your servant cannot taste what he eats or drinks. Nor can I any longer hear one voice or another. Why, then, should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant can barely cross the Jordan with my lord the king. Let my lord the king not repay me with this reward.

Let your servant remain, so that I may die in my own town beside the grave of my father and mother. Look, your servant, my son [?], is with you. Let him cross over with you, my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems right to you.”
The king said, “Let Bimham cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to me. And whatever you ask of me, I will do for you.”
All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king also crossed. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned to his own place.
The king crossed over to Gilgal, and Bimham crossed over with him. All the people of Judah crossed over with the king, along with half the people of Israel.

All Israel came to the king and said to him, “Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought you across the Jordan—you, the king, and your whole household, and all the people of Judah with you?”

All the people of Judah answered the people of Israel, “Because the king is closely related to us. Why are you upset about this? Have we eaten anything at the king’s expense, or has he given us a gift?”

The people of Israel answered the people of Judah, “We have ten shares in the king, and we have a greater claim on David than you do. Why have you treated us with contempt? We should have been the first to bring the king back.” But the words of the people of Judah were harsher than the words of the people of Israel.

A wicked man happened to be there, named Shammua son of Bichri, from Benjamin. He blew the trumpet and said, “We have no share with David, nor any inheritance with the son of Jesse. Go, everyone, to your tent!”
All the Israelites stopped following David and followed Shammua son of Bichri. But the people of Judah stayed with their king from the Jordan all the way to Jerusalem.

David came to his house in Jerusalem. The king took the ten concubines whom he had left to look after his house and confined them in a house under guard. He provided for them but did not have sexual relations with them. They remained in confinement until the day he died, living as widows.
The king said to Amasa, “Summon the people of Judah for me within three days, and you remain here.”
Amasa went to summon the people of Judah, but he delayed beyond the time appointed for him.

David said to Joab, “Now Shammua son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your master’s servants with you and pursue him, or he may find fortified towns for himself, establish himself in them, and gouge out our eyes.”
Joab’s companions, the nobles and the soldiers, and all the men went out after him. They left Jerusalem and pursued Shammua son of Bichri.

They reached the great stone at Gibeon, and Amasa came before them. Joab was wearing his military clothing, with a sword fastened at his waist like a razor. As he came forward, his hand fell on his sword.
Joab said to Amasa, “Peace to you, my brother!” Joab's hand took hold of Amasa's beard, and he kissed him.

Amasa did not guard against the sword in Joab’s hand. Joab struck him in the abdomen with it, and his intestines spilled onto the ground. He did not strike him a second time, and he died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Shammua son of Bichri.
One of Joab’s servants went and stood over him and said to him, “Whose man are you? If you are David’s, [?] after Joab.”

Amasa lay in the road, writhing in his blood. When the man saw that all the people were stopping to look, he dragged Amasa off the road and threw him into a field. He threw a rag over him, because he saw that everyone who passed him stopped.
Once he had dragged him off the road, everyone went on after Joab, pursuing Shammua son of Bichri to attack him.
They passed through all the tribes of Israel, through Abel and Beth-maacah and all the Berites, and went after him.
They came and encamped against him at Abel and Beth-maacah. They set ambushes against the town, and it was under siege. All the people with Joab were trying to bring down the wall.
A wise woman called from the wall, saying, “Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, ‘Come here so I can speak to you.’”
He approached her, and she said to him, “Are you Joab?” He said to her, “I am.” She said to him, “Listen to the words of your servant.” He said, “I am listening.”
The woman said, “In former times they used to say that they would first consult the prophets and only then destroy.
I have paid compensation for the harm. I belong to Israel, yet you seek to kill a child and its mother in Israel. Do not engulf the LORD’s inheritance.”
Joab answered her, “Far be it from me! I will neither swallow up nor destroy.

“That is not the case. Rather, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Shammua son of Bichri, has raised his hands against King David. Hand over him alone to me, and I will leave the town.” The woman said to Joab, “His head will now be thrown to you from the wall.”

The woman went to all the people with her wisdom. They cut off the head of Shammua son of Bichri and threw it from the wall to Joab. Joab blew the trumpet, and they withdrew from the town and went, each to his own tent. Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
