Joab was over the whole army of Israel, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the nobles and the soldiers.
Adoniram was in charge of the tribute, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Seraiah was the scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Aza from Jattir was also David’s priest.

There was a famine in David’s days for three years, year after year. David sought the LORD, and the LORD said, “It is because of Saul and his bloodstained household, because he killed the Gibeonites.”

The king summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. The Gibeonites were not Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites. The Israelites had sworn an oath to them, but Saul had sought to kill them in his zeal to purify the people of Israel and Judah.
David said to the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? How shall I make atonement to you, so that you will bless the LORD’s inheritance?”
The Gibeonites said to him, “It was not silver and gold that Saul and his household owed us, nor do we have anyone in Israel to put to death.” He said to them, “Whatever you say, I will do for you.”
They said to the king, “The man who destroyed us and planned to wipe us out, so that none of us would remain anywhere within Israel’s borders—
“Let seven men from among his sons be handed over to us, and we will sacrifice them before the Lord at Saul’s Ramah.” The king said to them, “I will hand them over.”
But the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan son of Saul because of the oath before the Lord that was between them, between David and Jonathan son of Saul.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Nadab daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai from Meholah.

He handed them over to the Gibeonites, who sacrificed them on the mountain before the Lord. All seven fell together. They were killed in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on the rock, from the beginning of the harvest until rain fell on them from heaven. She did not allow the birds of the sky to settle on them by day, or the wild animals by night.
David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine, had done.

David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the people of Jabesh-gilead. They had stolen them from the square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them on the day the Philistines killed Saul on Mount Gilboa.
He brought up the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from there, and they gathered the bones of those who had been killed.
They buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan in the land of Benjamin, at Zelzah, in the tomb of his father Kish. They did everything the king had commanded. After that, God showed favor to the land.
There was again war between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his servants to fight the Philistines, and David became afraid.
And Joab and Abishai [?] from the giants. The weight of his armor was three hundred weights of bronze, and he was armed with a new sword. He intended to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then David’s servants swore to him, saying, “You must not go out to battle with us, so that you do not extinguish the lamp of Israel.”
After that, there was again a battle with the Philistines at Gath. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saphar, who was one of the descendants of the giants.
There was again war between Israel and the Philistines. Elhanan son of Malaph, the weaver from Bethlehem, killed Goliath the Philistine. The shaft of his spear was as thick as a weaver’s beam.
There was again a battle at Gath. There was a giant there who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He too was descended from the giants.
He taunted Israel, and Jonadab son of Shammah, David's brother, killed him.
These four were descended from the giants in Gath, and they were delivered into the hands of David and his servants.
David’s song of praise. David spoke the words of this song of praise to the Lord on the day the Lord rescued him from the power of his enemies and from the power of Saul.
He said: I love you, Lord, my strength and my confidence. The Lord is my stronghold, my refuge, and my deliverer.
The mighty God in whom I place my hope, my helper and the horn of my salvation, my refuge, the one who rescues me from wicked people, and my savior.
I call upon the Lord, who is worthy of praise, and I am saved from my enemies.
For the cords of death surrounded me, and torrents of wickedness terrified me.
The cords of Sheol encircled me, and the snares of death confronted me.
In my distress I called to the Lord and cried out to my God. He heard my voice from his temple, and my cry before him reached his ears.
The earth shook and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains quaked and were shaken, because he was angry with them.
Smoke [?] in his anger, and fire blazed from his face, and coals [?] from it.
He bent the heavens and came down, with thick darkness beneath his feet.
He rode upon cherubim and flew; he soared on the wings of the wind.
He made darkness his hiding place, and his shelter surrounded him: dark waters in the clouds of the sky.
From the brightness of his shelter he made his clouds into hail and coals of fire.
The Lord thundered in heaven, and the Most High sounded his voice: hail and coals of fire.
He sent out his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightning flashes and threw them into confusion.
The springs of water appeared, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at your rebuke, Lord, and at the blast of the wind of your anger.
He reached down from on high and took hold of me; he drew me out of mighty waters.
He rescued me from my powerful enemies and from those who hated me, who were stronger than I was.
They confronted me on the day of my distress, but the Lord became my helper.
He brought me out into a spacious place and rescued me because he delighted in me.
The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness; he repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands.
For I kept the ways of the Lord and did not rebel against my God.
For all his judgments were before me, and I did not put his laws away from me.
I was blameless before him and guarded myself against sins.
The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness and according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.
With the good you will be good, and with the blameless person you will be blameless.
With the pure you will be pure, and with the crooked you will act crookedly.
For you will save the poor people and bring down haughty eyes.
You will light my lamp; the Lord my God will light up my darkness.
For through you I will charge against a troop, and through my God I will leap over a wall.
God's way is blameless; the word of the Lord is tested, and he helps everyone who trusts in him.
For there is no God apart from the Lord, and no one is mighty except our God.
God equipped me with strength and made my way blameless.
He made my feet like those of a deer and set me on my heights.
He trained my hands for battle and made my arms strong like a bronze bow.
You gave me the shield of salvation. Your right hand will support me, and your humility will make me great.
You made room for my steps beneath me so that my ankles would not give way.
I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until I have finished them off.
I will strike them so that they cannot rise, and they will fall beneath my feet.
You will equip me with strength in battle and make those who rise against me kneel beneath me.
You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and I will silence those who hate me.
They will cry out to the Lord, but they will have no rescuer; they will plead with the Lord, but he will not answer them.
I will grind them like dust before the wind, and I will trample them like mud in the streets.
You will deliver me from the disputes of the people and make me head over the nations; a people I did not know will serve me.
As soon as they hear me, they will obey me; foreigners will submit to me.
Foreigners will grow weak and limp away from their paths.
God lives! Blessed is the one who strengthens me! Exalted be God my Savior!
God gives me vengeance and subdues peoples beneath me.
He rescues me from my enemies. You also lift me above those who rise against me, and you rescue me from wicked men.
Therefore I will give thanks to you among the nations, my Lord, and sing praises to your name.
He grants great deliverance to his king and shows kindness to his anointed one, to David and his descendants forever.
These are David’s last words. David son of Jesse spoke; the man who established the yoke of his anointed and his God, the God of Jacob [?], the one who makes Israel’s songs sweet, spoke.
The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was on my tongue.
The God of Israel spoke, and the Mighty One of Israel said to me: “The one who rules over righteous people, who rules over those who fear God,
is like the morning light when the sun rises, a cloudless morning, from the brightness and from the rain that moistens the earth.”
My house was not like this with God, yet he established an everlasting covenant for me, with everything arranged and safeguarded, because he fulfills all my desire and all my commands.
But the wicked are all like hard thorns, for none of them can be taken by hand.
When a man approaches them, he gathers them with an axe handle and with iron, and they are burned up in the fire.
These are the names of David’s warriors. The one who occupied the first seat in the third rank was named Gadhu, the warrior who went down and killed eight hundred men at one time.

After him was Eleazar, the son of his father’s brother, when he went down among three warriors with David, when the Philistines taunted them and gathered there to do battle, and the men of Israel withdrew.
He stood and struck down the Philistines until his hand grew tired and clung to the hilt of his sword. The Lord brought deliverance that day, and the people returned after him to strip the dead.

After him arose Shammah son of Agee, from the king’s mountain. The Philistines had gathered to plunder livestock, and there was a plot of land there planted with lentils. The people fled before the Philistines.
He stood in the middle of the field, saved the crop, and struck down the Philistines. The LORD brought about a great deliverance through him.
Three of the warriors went down and came at harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, while the Philistine army was encamped in the Valley of the Giants.
David was then staying in the strongholds, and the Philistine commanders were stationed in Bethlehem.
David longed for water and said, “I wish someone would give me water to drink from the great well in the village of Bethlehem!”

The three mighty warriors broke through the Philistine camps and drew water from the great well in the village of Bethlehem. They took it and brought it to David, but he would not drink it. Instead, he poured it out before the Lord.
He said, “Far be it from me before the Lord to do this! These men went at the risk of their lifeblood.” He would not drink it. These were the deeds of the three mighty warriors.
Abishai, the brother of Joab son of Zeruiah, was chief of the thirty mighty warriors. He wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them.
He was more honored than the thirty and became their chief. He performed feats of valor equal to those of thirty men.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a mighty warrior from Kabzeel whose deeds were outstanding. He killed two mighty Moabite warriors. He also went down and killed a lion in a thicket on a snowy day.

He also killed an Egyptian, a handsome man. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went against him with a staff, seized the spear from the Egyptian’s hand, and killed him with his own spear.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada did these things, and he had fame and distinction among the thirty men.
He won victories equal to those of thirty men, and David appointed him to go out and come in.
Asahel, Joab’s brother, was among the thirty men.
Shammah from the King’s Mountain.
Helez the Paltite; Ira son of Ikkesh, from Tekoa.
Abiezer from Anathoth; Mebunnai from Hushah.
Zalmon from Mount Betha; Maharai from Topheth.
Heleb son of Baanah from Netophah; Ittai son of Ribai from Ramah of the Benjaminites.
Benaiah son of Pirathon from Geba; Hiddai from the ravines of Gaash.
Abi son of Abialmon from Gilead; Araboth from Hurim.
Elhanan from Shaalab; Jonathan from Beth-neshur.
Shammah from the Mount of Olives; Ahiam son of Ashdad from Edrei.
Eliphelet son of Hosbi from Maacah; Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite.
Hezrai from Mount Carmel; Iddai from Arub.
Negael son of Nathan from Zobah; Baanah from Gad.
Zelek from Ammon; Nahdai from Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah.
Ira from Jattir; Arab from Lachish.
Uriah the Hittite. All these servants of David numbered thirty-seven.
The Lord’s anger again grew fierce against Israel, and he stirred up David against them, saying to him, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”

David said to Joab and the army commanders who were with him, “Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba. Count the people for me and bring me their number and the total count of the people.”
Joab said to the king, “May the Lord your God increase the people a hundredfold, and may my lord the king see it with his own eyes! But why does my lord the king desire this thing?”
But the king’s command prevailed over Joab and the army commanders. So Joab and the army commanders went out from the king’s presence to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and came to Sharob, to the right of the town that is in the middle of the valley of Gad and Eliezer.

They came as far as Tyre and Sidon, to the land of the Canaanites, the land of the Hittites, and the land of the Jebusites. They traveled through the whole land and came to the land of Judah after thirty-eight days. They came to Dan and went around to Sidon.
They traveled throughout the whole land and came to Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days.

Joab brought the number and total count of the people to the king. The count for the house of Israel was eight hundred thousand mighty warriors who drew the sword, and the men of Judah numbered five hundred thousand.
David was troubled in his heart after he had counted the people. David said before the Lord, “I have sinned in what I have done. Even now I beg you, for I have acted very foolishly.”
David rose early in the morning, and the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet, saying to him:
“Go, tell David, ‘This is what the Lord says: I am bringing three calamities upon you. Choose for yourself, and I will carry it out against you.’”

Gad the prophet came to David and said to him, “The first calamity coming upon you is seven years of famine in your land; or you will be handed over to your enemy for three months, while he pursues you; or there will be three days of plague in your land. Now consider what answer you will give to the one who sent me to you.”

David answered Gad the prophet, “I am in great distress. It is better for us to be handed over into the hands of the Lord our God, for his mercies are great. Let us not be handed over into human hands.”
The Lord sent a plague upon Israel from morning until the sixth hour. Seventy thousand men died, from Dan to Beersheba.

The angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, but the Lord restrained the angel of death who was destroying the people. He said to him, “You have destroyed enough. Withdraw your hand.” The angel of the Lord was standing beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel destroying the people, he spoke before the Lord and said to the angel, “If I am the one who sinned and provoked anger, what have these innocent sheep done? Let your hand be against me and my father’s household.”
Gad the prophet came to David that same day and said to him, “Go up and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
David went up at Gad’s word, as the Lord had commanded him.
Araunah the Jebusite turned and saw King David and his servants passing along the road. Araunah fell down and bowed with his face to the ground before the king.
He said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David said, “To buy the threshing floor from you, to build an altar to the Lord so that the plague may be stopped among the people.”
Araunah said to David, “Let my lord the king take it. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledge and the yoke for firewood.”
Araunah gave all this to King David, and Araunah said to King David, “May the Lord your God bless you.”

David said to Araunah, “I will certainly buy it from you for a price. I will not offer the Lord my God a burnt offering that costs me nothing.” So David bought the garden’s threshing floor and the oxen for fifty staters.
David built an altar to the Lord there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. The Lord revealed himself in the land, and the plague was stopped among the house of Israel.
